title: Use the current NG-SIEM search repository contract
body:
Profile guidance

Inspect the selected client's target contract. A searchable target and a CQL source tag are separate namespaces; do not infer one from the other. Require explicit authorization, target and time window before execution.

Example:

```
#repo=example_repo
| head(10)
```

title: Interpret NG-SIEM execution metadata before reporting results
body:
Profile guidance

Inspect completion, errors, warnings, truncation, skipped results, returned columns and cleanup status. A successful start or done flag alone does not establish complete results. Distinguish static acceptance from execution and from an answer satisfying the analytic intent.

title: Pass NG-SIEM time windows as external search arguments
body:
Profile guidance

Require explicit time boundaries and timezone for the selected client. Keep search windows distinct from timestamp predicates inside the query. Preserve the intended interval and do not infer omitted boundaries.

title: Pair a field-presence count with a bare total in one query
body:
_pattern_

A zero from count(field=X) is ambiguous: the field may be absent, or no events matched at all. Compute the bare event count and the field-presence count in the same query so a zero presence next to a non-zero total reads unambiguously as 'field absent'. count(field=X) counts only events that contain X; count() counts every event; stats() runs both in one pass.

Syntax:

```
stats([count(as=total), count(field=<field>, as=with_field)])
```

- Caveat: A tag must be referenced with its # prefix; count(field="event.dataset") returns 0 wherever that name is a tag, which looks like an absent field (see cql:syntax:tags-not-fields).
- Caveat: A non-zero presence count says the field exists on some events, not that it is populated on all of them; compare with_field to total.
- Caveat: Run it over a narrow window first; it describes only the events in the window searched.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo | stats([count(as=total), count(field=example_field, as=with_field)])
```
total shows the events searched; with_field=0 and total>0 means the field is absent, total=0 means nothing matched.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=example_repo example_field=* | count()
```
Anti-pattern for diagnosis: a 0 cannot distinguish 'field absent' from 'no events in scope'.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:count`, `cql:function:stats`, `cql:syntax:missing-fields`, `cql:syntax:tags-not-fields`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-count.html (reviewed 2026-09-15); https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-stats.html (reviewed 2026-09-15); https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: Filter early; narrow scope and time before expensive work
body:
_performance_

For event searches, select the repository/view and the narrowest time window first, then apply selective tag and exact field filters, and only then perform expensive operations such as regular expressions over large text fields or wide aggregations. Reducing the candidate event set before costly stages is the single most important performance practice.

- Caveat: Source and table-definition functions keep their documented placement; filtering early does not mean placing an event filter before createEvents(), readFile(), or defineTable().
- Caveat: Row caps limit results returned, not data scanned: a broad predicate can still time out even with head()/sort limits.

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/writing-queries-write-best-practice.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: fieldset() lists the fields available in the result
body:
_function_

Aggregate that returns the list of fields available in the current context; useful when exploring an unfamiliar event set. Combining it with other functions can reduce the list.

Syntax:

```
fieldset()
```

- Caveat: Takes no parameters.
- Caveat: The returned field list is context specific; combining it with other functions such as an aggregate can reduce the list.
- Caveat: Aggregate function; incompatible with Filter Alerts (usable in Query, Live Query, Legacy Alert).
- Caveat: Output is more than one event.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo | fieldset()
```

Placeholder repo; lists fields seen.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo | groupBy([#type]) | fieldset()
```

After an aggregate the list shrinks to the aggregate's output fields (e.g. _count, #type).

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:groupBy`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-fieldset.html

title: head() returns the oldest events
body:
_function_

Returns up to limit (default 200) of the OLDEST events, sorted ascending by @timestamp (or @ingesttimestamp). Use tail() for the newest.

Syntax:

```
head([limit])
```

- `limit` (integer, optional, default '200') — Number of events to keep.

- Caveat: head() = oldest, tail() = newest - do not confuse them.
- Caveat: Capping returned rows does not reduce how much data is scanned.
- Caveat: head(10) is the same as head(limit=10). The default is 200 rows and the maximum is StateRowLimit (200,000 by default); limit=max uses StateRowLimit.
- Caveat: There is no limit() function or | limit stage in CQL; cap rows with head(n), tail(n), sort(..., limit=n) or table(..., limit=n).

Example (valid):

```
#repo=base_sensor #event_simpleName=UserLogon | head(50)
```

50 earliest matching logons.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=base_sensor #event_simpleName=UserLogon | limit(50)
```

No limit() function exists; write head(50) or sort(..., limit=50).

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:tail`, `cql:function:sort`, `cql:performance:result-caps`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-head.html

title: select() keeps only the listed fields per event
body:
_function_

Keeps only the named fields on each event and drops the rest, without aggregating or reordering. Use table() or groupBy() instead when you want summarized or sorted output.

Syntax:

```
select(fields)
```

- `fields` (array of strings, required) — Field names to retain on each event.

- Caveat: select() does not aggregate or sort - it is a per-event column projection.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 | select([@timestamp, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort])
```
Trim each event down to four fields.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:table`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-select.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: sort() orders rows and caps how many are returned
body:
_function_

Sorts events by one or more fields. order= sets asc/desc, type= sets numeric vs lexical ordering, and limit= (default 200) caps how many rows are returned. Sorting multiple fields uses arrays for field/order/type.

Syntax:

```
sort([field], [limit], [order], [reverse], [type])
```

- `field` (array of strings, optional, default '_count') — Field or fields to sort on.
- `limit` (integer, optional, default '200') — Maximum number of rows kept after sorting.
- `order` (array of strings, optional, default 'desc') — The order in which to sort.
- `type` (array of strings, optional, default 'number') — How values are compared when sorting, for example as numbers or as strings.

- Caveat: type defaults to number; sort a string field lexically with type=string or numbers will sort wrong.
- Caveat: limit caps returned rows only - it does not reduce scan cost or recover truncated groups.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | groupBy([ComputerName], function=count(as=c)) | sort(c, order=desc, limit=100)
```
Top 100 hosts by event count.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:head`, `cql:performance:result-caps`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-sort.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: table() builds a sortable, limited table of fields
body:
_function_

An aggregate that outputs a table of the specified fields, sorted by sortby (default @timestamp) and capped by limit (default 200). More flexible than select() when you want ordering and a row cap in one step.

Syntax:

```
table(fields, [limit], [order], [reverse], [sortby], [type])
```

- `fields` (array of strings, required) — Field names to show as columns.
- `limit` (integer, optional, default '200') — Maximum number of rows to show.
- `sortby` (array of strings, optional, default '@timestamp') — Names of fields to sort by.
- `order` (array of strings, optional, default 'desc') — Order to sort in.
- `type` (array of strings, optional, default 'number') — Type of the fields to sort.

- Caveat: table() is an aggregate and caps rows at limit; select() keeps every event but only trims columns.
- Caveat: limit defaults to 200; limit=max uses StateRowLimit (200,000 by default). Rows beyond the cap are not returned.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | table([@timestamp, ComputerName, FileName, CommandLine], sortby=@timestamp, order=desc, limit=200)
```
Recent processes as a column-selected, time-sorted table.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:select`, `cql:function:sort`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-table.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: tail() returns the most recent events
body:
_function_

Returns up to limit (default 200) of the MOST RECENT events, sorted by @timestamp (or @ingesttimestamp). Use head() for the oldest.

Syntax:

```
tail([limit])
```

- `limit` (integer, optional, default '200') — Number of events to keep from the end.

- Caveat: tail() = newest, head() = oldest.
- Caveat: A row cap is not a scan-cost limit; narrow the filter/time window to control cost.
- Caveat: head(10) is the same as head(limit=10). The default is 200 rows and the maximum is StateRowLimit (200,000 by default); limit=max uses StateRowLimit.
- Caveat: There is no limit() function or | limit stage in CQL; cap rows with head(n), tail(n), sort(..., limit=n) or table(..., limit=n).

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=DetectionSummaryEvent | tail(100)
```
100 most recent detection events.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:head`, `cql:performance:result-caps`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-tail.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: base64Decode() decodes a Base64 field to a string
body:
_function_

Decodes the Base64 value in a field and interprets the bytes as text using a chosen character set. Useful for reading encoded command arguments after extracting them into their own field.

Syntax:

```
base64Decode([as], [charset], field)
```

- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_base64Decode') — Field that receives the decoded string.
- `charset` (string, optional, default 'UTF-8') — Charset used to turn the decoded bytes into text: ISO-8859-1, UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE or UTF-8.
- `field` (string (fieldname), required) — The field containing the Base64 values to decode. The name field can be omitted.

- Caveat: Decoded bytes are interpreted with charset; for binary data the page says to use ISO-8859-1.
- Caveat: No output field is created when the input is not valid Base64.
- Caveat: Characters outside the Base64 alphabet are ignored.
- Caveat: Bytes that are not valid in the chosen charset are replaced by a placeholder character, one per invalid code point.
- Caveat: The CQL page prescribes no charset, but Microsoft documents -EncodedCommand payloads as UTF-16LE for both powershell.exe and pwsh; see cql:pattern:decode-encoded-powershell.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 FileName=powershell.exe | regex("(?i)-(?:enc|encodedcommand)\\s+(?<enc_b64>[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)", field=CommandLine) | base64Decode(field=enc_b64, charset="UTF-16LE", as=decoded_cmd)
```

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | base64Decode(CommandLine, encoding=UTF-16LE)
```

encoding is not a parameter; the parameter is charset.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:regex`, `cql:function:eval`, `cql:syntax:regex-literals`, `cql:pattern:decode-encoded-powershell`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-base64decode.html

title: concat() joins the values of several fields
body:
_function_

Concatenates the values of the listed fields into one output field. It only joins fields, not string literals; use format() to mix literals and fields.

Syntax:

```
concat([as], field)
```

- `field` (array of strings (fieldnames), required) — Fields to concatenate. The argument name can be omitted.
- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_concat') — Name of the field that receives the result.

- Caveat: Cannot combine arbitrary strings, or strings and fields; use format("%s/%s", field=[a,b], as=out) for that.
- Caveat: The page recommends a consistent format and a separator so the parts can be split apart later.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | concat([ComputerName, FileName], as=host_file)
```
Join two fields into host_file.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | concat([ComputerName, "|", FileName], as=host_file)
```
concat() cannot mix string literals and fields; use format("%s|%s", field=[ComputerName,FileName], as=host_file).

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:format`, `cql:function:lower`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-concat.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: length() returns the character length of a field
body:
_function_

Measures the length of a field's string value and stores it in an output field - useful for spotting unusually long values such as command lines. Length counts Java characters, not grapheme clusters.

Syntax:

```
length([as], field)
```

- `field` (string (fieldname), required) — Input field to measure. The argument name can be omitted.
- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_length') — Name of the output field.

- Caveat: Counts Java characters (the page's wording); for grapheme clusters the page points to text:length().
- Caveat: The page does not mention bytes.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | length(CommandLine, as=cmd_len) | cmd_len > 2000 | table([ComputerName, FileName, cmd_len])
```
Long command lines; the 2000 threshold is illustrative and must be tuned.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | length(CommandLine) | _length > 2000
```
Default output field is _length.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:table`, `cql:function:lower`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-length.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: lower() / upper() change the case of a field
body:
_function_

lower() writes the lowercase form of a field's value to an output field; upper() does the same in uppercase. The result goes to a new field (_lower / _upper) unless as= names one, so a later filter must reference that output field.

Syntax:

```
lower([as], field, [locale], [type])
```

- `field` (string (fieldname), required) — Input field whose value is converted to lower case. The argument name can be omitted.
- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_lower') — Name of the output field.
- `locale` (string, optional, default 'system locale') — ISO 639 language with optional ISO 3166 country, e.g. en or en_US.
- `type` (string, optional) — Documented with the same description as locale (ISO 639 language and ISO 3166 country); the page does not say how it differs.

- Caveat: upper([as], field, [locale]) has the same shape with as defaulting to _upper; upper() has no type parameter.
- Caveat: Output goes to as (default _lower / _upper), not back into the input field; filter on the output field name, not the original.
- Caveat: Without locale the system locale is used; the page says the locale matters most for non-Latin alphabets.
- Caveat: field may be passed positionally: lower(FileName) is equivalent to lower(field=FileName).

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | lower(FileName, as=fn_lower) | fn_lower="powershell.exe" | groupBy([fn_lower], function=count())
```
Normalize case into a named field, then filter on that field.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | upper(FileName, as=fn_upper) | fn_upper="CMD.EXE"
```
upper() with the same as= pattern.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | lower(FileName) | FileName="powershell.exe"
```
lower() without as= writes to _lower; FileName is unchanged, so this is still a case-sensitive match on the original field. Filter on _lower or set as=.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:troubleshooting:case-sensitive-equality`, `cql:syntax:regex-literals`, `cql:function:format`, `cql:function:eval`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-lower.html (reviewed 2026-10-21); https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-upper.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: shannonEntropy() computes the entropy of a string field
body:
_function_

Calculates an entropy measure for the characters in a field, so more random-looking strings score higher. Treat it as one signal to combine with other filters, not a verdict.

Syntax:

```
shannonEntropy([as], field)
```

- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_shannonentropy') — Name of the output field that stores the result.
- `field` (string (fieldname), required) — Name of the input field. The name field can be omitted.

- Caveat: The docs say the entropy value alone is not conclusive and context matters; use it for further filtering or with other aggregate functions.
- Caveat: The docs list no limits.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | shannonEntropy(field=FileName, as=name_entropy) | name_entropy > 4.5
```

Score executable names, then keep high scorers. 4.5 is an illustrative threshold, not from the docs; tune against real data.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | name_entropy := shannonEntropy(FileName)
```

Assignment form with the field name omitted.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | entropy(FileName)
```

There is no entropy() function; the function is shannonEntropy().

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:eval`, `cql:function:regex`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-shannonentropy.html

title: splitString() splits a field into an array by a string or regex
body:
_function_

Splits a field's value on a separator (string or regular expression) into indexed fields named <as>[0], <as>[1], ... With index= it emits only that element. Defaults: field @rawstring, output _splitstring.

Syntax:

```
splitString([as], by, [field], [index])
```

- `by` (string or regex, required) — Literal text or regular expression to split on.
- `field` (string (fieldname), optional, default '@rawstring') — Field that needs splitting. The argument name can be omitted.
- `index` (integer, optional) — Return only the element at this index; negative values count from the end, so -1 is the last.
- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_splitstring') — Name for the selected element.

- Caveat: Output is an array: with as=part the fields are part[0], part[1], ...; with the default they are _splitstring[0], _splitstring[1], ....
- Caveat: by is a regular expression, so metacharacters (asterisk, pipe and so on) need escaping; write a multi-character separator as a group, for example (\*\|\*).
- Caveat: The page chains splitString() with split() to turn the array into one event per element; split() is a separate function.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | arg0 := splitString(field=CommandLine, by=" ", index=0) | groupBy([arg0], function=count())
```
First space-separated token of the command line.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | splitString(field=CommandLine, by=" ", as=arg)
```
Without index= the parts land in indexed fields arg[0], arg[1], ...

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | splitString(field=CommandLine, by="*|*")
```
by is a regular expression: * and | are special and must be escaped, and a multi-character separator belongs in a group.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:regex-literals`, `cql:function:regex`, `cql:function:format`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-splitstring.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: urlDecode() URL-decodes a field value
body:
_function_

Reverses percent-encoding in a field and stores the decoded text in a new field. Handy before matching on URLs or command lines that carry encoded characters.

Syntax:

```
urlDecode([as], field)
```

- `as` (string (fieldname), optional, default '_urldecode') — Names the output field.
- `field` (string (fieldname), required) — Names the input field whose value is URL-decoded. The name field can be omitted.

- Caveat: Without as, the result is written to _urldecode.
- Caveat: The docs list no further limits or caveats.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | urlDecode(field=CommandLine, as=cmd_decoded)
```
Decoded copy of the command line in a named field.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | cmd_decoded := urlDecode(CommandLine)
```
Assignment form with the field name omitted.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | urlDecode(CommandLine, into=cmd_decoded)
```
into is not a parameter; use as= or :=.

See also: `cql:function:eval`, `cql:function:replace`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-urldecode.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: Comments use // and /* ... */
body:
_syntax_

CQL supports // for single-line comments and /* ... */ for multi-line comments. Use them to annotate saved queries and correlation rules for easier triage and handoff.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon // interactive logons only
| groupBy([UserName])
```
Single-line comment inside a query.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:concept:pipeline`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: Comparison operators: = != like < <= > >= /regex/
body:
_syntax_

The left side of a comparison is a field name and the right side a value. String equality (=) matches the whole value and is case-sensitive, and a * in the value makes it a whole-value glob (see cql:syntax:wildcard-and-like); != negates; like matches a substring with * wildcards; <, <=, >, >= compare numbers; /regex/ matches a pattern. Use the wildcard() function for flexible wildcard matching.

- Caveat: = is case-sensitive and, for a value without *, exact - a case or partial-match mismatch returns nothing.
- Caveat: The left side is always read as a field name: `200 = statuscode` looks for a field literally named 200.
- Caveat: Field names may be quoted strings. Double-quote names containing spaces or hyphens, for example `"user name"=*` or `"event-action"="login"`; preserve the exact name discovered in the data.

Example (valid):

```
statuscode = 404
```

Exact match.

Example (valid):

```
ImageFileName like "*\\powershell.exe"
```

Substring match with wildcard.

Example (valid):

```
Severity >= 70
```

Numeric comparison.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:concept:boolean-precedence`, `cql:syntax:wildcard-and-like`, `cql:function:in`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/query-operation-troubleshooting.html; https://library.humio.com/lql-grammar.pdf

title: Expression-context equality (==) and test()
body:
_syntax_

In a filter, equality is a single = with a field name on the left (statuscode=404). Inside an expression context - the boolean argument to test() or a computed comparison - use == for equality, as in a programming language. test() filters events on an arbitrary boolean expression rather than a single field=value predicate, so it can compare two fields or a computed value.

Syntax:

```
test(expression)   e.g. test(a == b)
```

- Caveat: Do not conflate the two: = is the filter/search equality operator; == is the expression-context equality operator used inside test() and computed comparisons.
- Caveat: test() expresses comparisons a bare field=value filter cannot, such as comparing two fields to each other.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 | test(LocalPort == RemotePort)
```
Compare two fields - not expressible with a plain field=value filter.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | test(RssBytes / 1024 > 500)
```
Filter on a computed expression.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:comparison-operators`, `cql:function:eval`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15); https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-test.html (reviewed 2026-10-25)

title: Create or overwrite fields with := (or as=)
body:
_syntax_

New fields are added with the := assignment shorthand (name := expression), with a function's as= parameter, via regex named capture groups, or with eval(). Assigning to an existing name overwrites it. =~ assigns the result of a function such as join().

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ratio := RssBytes / 1024
```
Inline computed field.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:eval`, `cql:function:rename`

title: A comparison on an absent field fails (except !=)
body:
_syntax_

If an event does not contain the field being compared, every comparison fails - except !=. To select events that lack a field, use `foo != *` or the equivalent `not (foo = *)`; to require a field's presence use `foo = *`.

- Caveat: This is why an added filter can make results vanish: events missing that field are dropped, not kept.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon UserName != *
```
Events with no UserName field.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon UserName = *
```
Events that have a UserName field.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:default`, `cql:troubleshooting:missing-field-filters-out`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: Regex literals and re2j-style syntax
body:
_syntax_

A field can be matched against a regular expression with Field=/pattern/flags or via the regex()/replace() functions. CrowdStrike CQL uses JitRex, closely following re2j (Java-like) regex syntax. Backslashes must be escaped inside quoted strings.

- Caveat: Inside a double-quoted string a backslash is doubled (\\d), but inside a /.../ literal it is written once (\d).
- Caveat: Regex over large text fields is expensive - filter first.

Example (valid):

```
CommandLine=/-enc\s+[A-Za-z0-9+\/=]{20,}/i
```
Case-insensitive regex literal with flag.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:regex`, `cql:function:replace`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: Tags are not fields - reference a tag with its prefix
body:
_syntax_

A parser promotes some of its fields to tags (its fields_to_tag set), and a tag is a different namespace from a parsed field: it is referenced by its prefixed name (#event.dataset, #repo, #type) or, for CrowdStrike CQL's own metadata tags, by the @-prefixed name (@sourcetype). The unprefixed spelling of a tagged field does not exist, so count(field="event.dataset") returns 0 and groupBy([event.dataset]) yields nothing - with no error, because an absent field is a legal thing to ask about. Reference a tag exactly as the parser's documentation spells it; an environment reference, when one exists, marks tagged fields [tag].

- Caveat: This fails silently and looks like empty data rather than a mistake: the query is valid CQL, the field genuinely is absent under that name, and the result is a confident zero.
- Caveat: Which fields are tags is per-parser, not universal - one source may tag event.dataset while another carries it as an ordinary field. Check the parser's documented tag list (or an environment reference, if one exists) instead of assuming.
- Caveat: Filtering on a tag is the cheapest way to scope a search, so lead with the tag filter (#repo=..., #type=...) before any field predicate.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo
| groupBy([#event.dataset], function=count())
```

Group on the tag, using its # prefix.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=example_repo
| count(field="event.dataset")
```

Anti-pattern: returns 0 wherever event.dataset is a tag. No error is raised - the unprefixed name simply does not exist.

Applicability: CrowdStrike NG-SIEM / CrowdStrike CQL / The rule is universal; the tag set is parser-specific and comes from each parser's declared fields_to_tag list.

See also: `cql:syntax:missing-fields`, `cql:troubleshooting:dataset-tag-unset`, `cql:function:groupBy`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax.html

title: Wildcards, like, and the wildcard() function
body:
_syntax_

* is the wildcard character. Under bare =, a value that contains * is a glob that must match the whole field value, whether or not it is quoted: gid="S-1-5-21-*-512". The like operator matches the pattern anywhere inside the value (a substring match) and also understands *. The wildcard() function adds options such as ignoreCase. Inside a /regex/ literal * is a quantifier, not a glob.

- Caveat: Do not write a glob inside a regex literal: * repeats the preceding regex expression rather than acting as a glob wildcard. See cql:troubleshooting:regex-glob-and-substring.

Example (valid):

```
FileName like "*.exe"
```

Matches anywhere in the value.

Example (valid):

```
gid="S-1-5-21-*-512"
```

Whole-value glob under =; the * can match several characters.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
gid=/S-1-5-21-*-512/
```

Anti-pattern: a regex literal. The * repeats the preceding hyphen, so this matches S-1-5-21-512 and misses S-1-5-21-111-222-333-512.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:comparison-operators`, `cql:function:regex`, `cql:troubleshooting:regex-glob-and-substring`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html

title: createEvents() generates synthetic events from strings
body:
_function_

Source/aggregate function that emits one event per input string, with the string as @rawstring and no extracted fields. Add kvParse() or parseJson() to turn the strings into fields. Data exists only for the query; nothing is stored in the repository.

Syntax:

```
createEvents(rawstring)
```

- `rawstring` (string (interpreted as an array of strings), required) — The events to emit. Each string becomes the @rawstring of one event and is not processed further. The parameter name may be omitted.

- Caveat: Aggregator: it discards incoming events and outputs only the generated ones, so it is not a filter on an existing stream; the docs examples always put it at the start of the query.
- Caveat: Generated events have no extracted fields; add kvParse() or parseJson() to extract them.
- Caveat: The data is temporary: it exists only for the duration of the query and nothing is stored in the repository.
- Caveat: Special characters inside the strings must be backslash-escaped (newlines, tabs, quotes, backslashes, Unicode code points); quotes inside JSON strings must be escaped too.
- Caveat: Docs list the function type as Aggregate and Source, incompatible with Filter Alerts; compatible contexts are Query, Live Query and Legacy Alert.
- Caveat: The docs page states no event-count limit, no size limit, and no explicit must-be-first rule; do not assume any.

Example (valid):

```
createEvents(["FileName=powershell.exe", "FileName=notepad.exe"]) | kvParse()
```

Two synthetic events, each with a FileName field after kvParse().

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
createEvents(["FileName=powershell.exe"]) | FileName=powershell.exe
```

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=base_sensor #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | createEvents(["a=1"])
```

createEvents() is an aggregator that discards incoming events; the base_sensor filter is thrown away. Start the query with it.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language / Function type Aggregate and Source; incompatible with Filter Alerts.

See also: `cql:function:kvParse`, `cql:function:parseJson`, `cql:function:readFile`, `cql:function:correlate`, `cql:pattern:offline-test-createevents`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-createevents.html

title: Construct temporary query input with createEvents()
body:
createEvents constructs temporary input inside a query and replaces the incoming event stream. Parse its raw strings before referring to extracted fields. These temporary values do not establish deployment fields, tags or event ordering.

Example:

```
createEvents(["FileName=powershell.exe", "FileName=notepad.exe"])
| kvParse()
| groupBy([FileName], function=count())
```

Parsing must precede filters or aggregates that read FileName. Keep any source selectors for existing repository events in a separate query context.

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-createevents.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-definetable.html

title: findTimestamp() detects a timestamp in text
body:
_function_

Searches a field (default @rawstring) for a recognizable timestamp and writes it as epoch milliseconds, adding an error field if none is found. Designed for generic parsers that handle several formats.

Syntax:

```
findTimestamp([addErrors], [as], [field], [timezone], [timezoneAs], [timezoneField])
```

- `addErrors` (boolean, optional, default 'true') — Add an error field when no timestamp is found.
- `as` (string, optional, default '@timestamp') — Output field for the timestamp (epoch ms). Keep the default in parsers.
- `field` (string, optional, default '@rawstring') — Field to scan for a timestamp.
- `timezone` (string, optional) — Default timezone when the timestamp has none; if unset and timezoneField has no valid zone, the timestamp is not parsed.
- `timezoneAs` (string, optional, default '@timezone') — Output field for the parsed timezone. Keep the default in parsers.
- `timezoneField` (string, optional, default '@timezone') — Field holding a per-event default timezone.

- Caveat: Intended for generic parsers handling multiple event types; if the format is known, the page recommends parseTimestamp().
- Caveat: Detection looks only at the first 128 characters, so a timestamp that starts later is missed.
- Caveat: Leap seconds are ignored; two-digit years are read as 2013-2099.
- Caveat: Only the first three sub-second digits are kept (millisecond precision).
- Caveat: In parsers keep as and timezoneAs at defaults; in queries output can go to custom fields.
- Caveat: For daylight-saving ambiguity the page recommends giving timezone as an offset.

Example (valid):

```
findTimestamp(field=date, timezone="Europe/London")
```
Docs example: timestamp located in a field named date.

Example (valid):

```
findTimestamp(as="datetime", timezoneAs="tz")
```
Docs example for query use: output to custom fields.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
findTimestamp(format="yyyy-MM-dd")
```
No format parameter; the function auto-detects. For a known format use parseTimestamp().

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:formatTime`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-findtimestamp.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: formatTime() renders a timestamp as a formatted string
body:
_function_

Formats an epoch value (default @timestamp) into a string using Java Formatter-style date/time escapes, in a chosen timezone and locale. unit controls whether the input is read as seconds or milliseconds.

Syntax:

```
formatTime(as, [field], format, [locale], [timezone], [unit])
```

- `as` (fieldname, required) — Name of the output field.
- `field` (double, optional, default '@timestamp') — 64-bit integer since the Unix epoch, read as seconds or milliseconds depending on unit.
- `format` (string, required) — Date/time format string built from a limited set of Java conversions; the argument name may be left out.
- `locale` (string, optional) — Locale such as US or en_GB.
- `timezone` (timezone, optional, default 'UTC') — Zone to render in, for example GMT, EST or Europe/London; UTC when not given.
- `unit` (fixed values, optional, default 'auto') — Whether field is read as seconds or milliseconds: auto, milliseconds, seconds.

- Caveat: Format strings support only part of the Java Formatter's date and time conversions (the docs link the Java 11 Formatter); listed symbols include %H, %M, %S, %L, %s, %Q, %F, %T, %z, %Z.
- Caveat: unit=auto reads values up to 100,000,000,000 as seconds and larger values as milliseconds; unit=milliseconds and unit=seconds force the reading.
- Caveat: When unit is set, the input must be an integer (long), not a float; for fractional values, extract the integer digits with regex() first, as the docs suggest.
- Caveat: If no timezone is given UTC is used.
- Caveat: Millisecond precision is dropped from ISO 8601 output unless the format includes a millisecond specifier.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ts := formatTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", field=@timestamp, timezone=UTC)
```
Human-readable event time; @timestamp is the grounded timestamp field.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | formatTime("%FT%T%z", as=iso, field=@timestamp, unit=milliseconds)
```
ISO 8601 output with explicit millisecond input.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ts := formatTime("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss", field=@timestamp)
```
Format uses Java Formatter %-escapes, not SimpleDateFormat letters.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:timeChart`, `cql:function:bucket`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-formattime.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: @timestamp and _bucket are epoch milliseconds
body:
Profile guidance

Verify timestamp units before subtracting, scaling, comparing or formatting values. Use explicit unit arguments where available. The profile checks signed-long literals for explicit seconds/milliseconds arguments and retains uncertainty for dynamic expressions.

Anti-pattern — do not use:

```
... | test((t2-t1)*1000 <= 3600000)
```

Example:

```
... | test(t2-t1 <= 3600000)
```

title: case { } runs the first matching clause, with a * catch-all
body:
_syntax_

A case block holds semicolon-terminated clauses, each a pipeline (typically a filter followed by an assignment). For each event, clauses are tried top to bottom and the first one that matches runs. Add a final * clause to handle everything else.

Syntax:

```
case {
  pipeline1;
  pipeline2;
  * | pipeline3;
}
```

- Caveat: A clause matches if its pipeline returns events; clauses are evaluated top to bottom, one at a time, until one matches, independently per event.
- Caveat: If no clause matches, the event is dropped. Add a final * clause to keep the remaining events.
- Caveat: The * clause may set a default value or do nothing; omitting it entirely (not the same as a no-op *) removes non-matching events.
- Caveat: Each clause is a full pipeline, so it can both filter and transform.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | case { FileName="powershell.exe" | proc_class := "shell"; FileName="cmd.exe" | proc_class := "shell"; * | proc_class := "other" }
```

Two named classes plus a * default, so every ProcessRollup2 event gets a proc_class value.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | case { FileName="powershell.exe" | proc_class := "shell"; FileName="cmd.exe" | proc_class := "shell" }
```

No * clause: every event matching neither FileName is dropped from the results, not left unlabelled.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:if`, `cql:function:default`, `cql:syntax:field-assignment`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-conditional.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-if.html

title: coalesce() returns the first non-null expression
body:
_function_

Checks a list of expressions left to right and stores the first non-null result in an output field. By default empty strings are skipped.

Syntax:

```
coalesce([as], expressions, [ignoreEmpty])
```

- `as` (string, optional, default '_coalesce') — Names the field that stores the selected value, if a non-null value is found.
- `expressions` (array of expressions, required) — Candidates to check. The first non-null result, read left to right, is used. The name expressions can be omitted.
- `ignoreEmpty` (boolean, optional, default 'true') — When true, empty strings are skipped. Set false to allow empty strings to be returned.

- Caveat: Field names containing characters that cannot be written bare (spaces, hyphens) must be wrapped in getField(), e.g. coalesce([getField("host-name"), "example.com"]).
- Caveat: Order matters: the first non-null candidate wins, so put the preferred source first.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | coalesce([ParentBaseFileName, FileName], as=proc_label)
```
Falls back to FileName when ParentBaseFileName is missing or empty.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language / Docs list availability from 1.159.0.

See also: `cql:function:default`, `cql:function:if`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-coalesce.html (reviewed 2026-10-21)

title: default() fills a missing or empty field
body:
_function_

Sets field to value when the field is absent (or empty, with replaceEmpty=true). Existing non-empty values are kept. Useful before grouping so missing values fall into a named bucket instead of disappearing.

Syntax:

```
default(field, [replaceEmpty], value)
```

- `field` (array of strings, required) — Field or fields that should receive a fallback value.
- `value` (string, required) — Fallback value written when the field has none.
- `replaceEmpty` (boolean, optional, default 'false') — With true, an empty string also counts as missing and is replaced.

- Caveat: Without replaceEmpty=true, only absent fields are filled, not present-but-empty ones.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon | default(field=UserName, value="(none)") | groupBy([UserName], function=count())
```
Give missing usernames a label before grouping.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:groupBy`, `cql:troubleshooting:missing-field-filters-out`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-default.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: eval() computes a new field from an expression
body:
_function_

Computes a new field from an expression. The expression must start with an assignment (name=expr); the shorthand `name := expr` means the same. It can read other fields, use arithmetic and comparison operators, and call functions.

Syntax:

```
eval()
```

- Caveat: The eval string must start with an assignment; use := as the inline shorthand.
- Caveat: Assigning to an existing field name overwrites it.
- Caveat: round() takes a field name, not an expression, and has no decimals parameter; use format("%.2f", field=x) for fixed decimals.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | eval(cmd_len := length(CommandLine)) | sort(cmd_len, order=desc, limit=50)
```

Derive a numeric field, then rank by it.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:if`, `cql:syntax:field-assignment`, `cql:troubleshooting:eval-missing-input`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-eval.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-format.html

title: format() builds a printf-style string field
body:
_function_

Creates a new field containing a printf-style formatted string built from one or more input fields. Pass multiple fields as an array in field=[a,b].

Syntax:

```
format([as], field, format, [timezone])
```

- `format` (string, required) — Format specifiers that build the output string from the input field or fields.
- `field` (array of strings, required) — The fields to format.
- `as` (string, optional, default '_format') — Name of the field that receives the result.
- `timezone` (string, optional) — Timezone used when the format renders dates or times.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon | format(format="%s@%s", field=[UserName, ComputerName], as=user_host)
```
Combine two fields into one label.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:eval`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-format.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: if() chooses between two expressions on a condition
body:
_function_

Returns then when condition is true and else otherwise, similar to a ternary operator. Because it is an expression, if() can be embedded inside other functions and assignments, unlike a case/match statement.

Syntax:

```
if([as], condition, else, then)
```

- `condition` (expression, required) — The conditional expression to evaluate.
- `then` (expression, required) — The consequent statement to execute.
- `else` (expression, required) — The alternative statement to execute.
- `as` (string, optional, default '_if') — Name of the field that receives the result.

- Caveat: condition, then, and else are all required.
- Caveat: Regex conditions are supported through regex(), as in statusClass := if(regex("^4", field=statuscode), then="client error", else="other"). Do not substitute a blanket ban on regex in if().
- Caveat: For multi-branch logic use a case statement instead of nested if().

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=DetectionSummaryEvent | sev_band := if(Severity>=70, then="high", else="low")
```
Inline conditional assignment.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:eval`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-if.html (reviewed 2026-10-26)

title: rename() renames one or more fields
body:
_function_

Renames a field to a new name. Rename several at once by passing arrays. Handy for normalizing field names across repositories before a join or a unified table.

Syntax:

```
rename([as], field)
```

- `field` (array of strings, required) — Field to rename; used when the new name is given through as.
- `as` (string, optional) — New name for the field; applies when a single field is named in field.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=detections | rename(field=Attributes.name, as=rule_name)
```
Give a nested field a short alias.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:eval`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-rename.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: replace() does regex substitution within a field
body:
_function_

Replaces each substring of a field matching a regular expression with a replacement string, writing to as (default: back into the input field). Uses CrowdStrike CQL's re2j-style regex syntax.

Syntax:

```
replace([as], [field], [flags], regex, [replacement], [with])
```

- `regex` (string, required) — The regular expression to match.
- `with` (string, optional, default '""') — Text that replaces each match.
- `field` (string, optional, default '@rawstring') — Field the replacement runs on.
- `flags` (string, optional, default 'm') — Specifies other regex flags.
- `as` (string, optional, default 'input field') — Field that receives the replaced string.

- Caveat: Default field is @rawstring; set field= to target a specific field.
- Caveat: Backreferences in the replacement use the regex capture groups.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | replace("\\d+", with="N", field=CommandLine, as=cmd_masked)
```
Mask digit runs into a new field.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:regex`, `cql:syntax:regex-literals`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-replace.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: eval() skips the target when an input field is missing
body:
Profile guidance

Resolve missing-input policy before scalar computation. The profile treats nullable outputs conservatively and does not infer target presence from an expression alone. Use an explicit default or coalescing rule when the intended analysis needs a fallback.

Anti-pattern — do not use:

```
... | eval(c=a+1)
```

Example:

```
... | default(field=a, value=0) | eval(c=a+1)
```

title: Empty results from case-sensitive equality
body:
_troubleshooting_

= is exact and case-sensitive, so UserName=Alice will not match 'alice'. When an exact filter returns nothing unexpectedly, suspect case or partial-match. Use a /regex/i literal or an ignoreCase parameter for case-insensitive matching.

Example (valid):

```
UserName=/^alice$/i
```
Case-insensitive exact match via regex flag.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:comparison-operators`, `cql:function:in`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: Check dataset-tag presence before grouping
body:
Profile guidance

Check tag presence for the selected sources and time window before using a tag as a completeness boundary. Compare scoped totals with an explicitly chosen baseline. Inspect parser-error populations separately and do not infer tag presence from a parser declaration.

Anti-pattern as a completeness count:

```
#repo=example_repo
| groupBy([#event.dataset], function=count(as=events))
```

Example:

```
#repo=example_repo
| count(as=total)
```

Example:

```
#repo=example_repo
| groupBy([#type, #event.dataset], function=count(as=events))
```

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/query-operation-troubleshooting.html

title: Distinct counts are estimates; use groupBy then count() for an exact figure
body:
_troubleshooting_

count(distinct=true) does not keep every value in memory; for many distinct values it returns an estimate, not an exact figure. The docs give the typical standard error as under 2% but state the algorithm gives no guarantee on relative error, and the deviation is larger below 100 distinct values. For an exact distinct count, group on the field and count the groups: groupBy([field], limit=max) | count(). Keep count(distinct=true) for large populations where an estimate is acceptable.

- Caveat: The exact method is itself bounded by the groupBy group cap: with the default limit, groups beyond 20,000 are dropped and the count is silently low. limit=max raises the cap to its documented maximum. See cql:performance:groupby-explicit-limit.
- Caveat: The count docs do not name the estimation algorithm; do not cite one.
- Caveat: The docs note that with fewer than 100 distinct values the relative deviation grows, so small counts can be proportionally further off.
- Caveat: For an exact distinct count per group, the first groupBy() holds one row per (group, value) pair, so its cardinality is the pair count. That is far larger than either field alone and hits the group limit sooner.

Example (valid):

```
... | groupBy([host], function=count(field=user, distinct=true, as=users))
```

Per-host distinct users - estimated at high cardinality.

Example (valid):

```
... | groupBy([user], limit=max) | count(as=distinct_users)
```

Exact distinct count: one row per user, then count the rows. limit=max raises the group cap; a population above the documented maximum still truncates.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | groupBy([FileName, aid], limit=max) | groupBy([FileName], function=count(as=distinct_hosts), limit=max)
```

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:count`, `cql:function:groupBy`, `cql:performance:groupby-explicit-limit`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-count.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-groupby.html

title: A guessed tag value returns a silent zero
body:
_troubleshooting_

Tag filters such as #type=<value> are exact. A value that is guessed rather than read from the data matches nothing and returns zero rows with no error. Treat that zero as inconclusive. Discover the real values first by grouping on the tag in the repository, then rerun the original query changing only the tag value, so the comparison is controlled.

- Caveat: Change one thing per run: if the filter, window and repository change together, a non-zero result no longer shows the guessed value was the cause.
- Caveat: Which tag values exist is per-repository and per-source; read them from the data (or an environment reference, if one exists) instead of inferring them from another repository.
- Caveat: Run the discovery over a narrow window; it lists only the values present in that window.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo | groupBy([#type], function=count())
```
Discovery step: list the real #type values and their counts.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo #type=<value_from_discovery> | count()
```
Controlled rerun: same query, only the tag value replaced by one observed above.

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=example_repo #type=guessed-value | count()
```
Anti-pattern: a guessed exact tag value; a 0 here proves nothing.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:tags-not-fields`, `cql:troubleshooting:case-sensitive-equality`, `cql:pattern:field-presence-vs-total`

title: Adding a field filter silently dropped events
body:
_troubleshooting_

If results shrink or vanish after adding a field predicate, remember that events lacking that field fail every comparison except !=. Confirm the field exists on the events (foo = *) or fill it with default() before filtering/grouping.

Example (valid):

```
#event_simpleName=UserLogon UserName=* | groupBy([UserName])
```
Require the field first to see how many events actually have it.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:syntax:missing-fields`, `cql:function:default`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/syntax-operators.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: regex() over a JSON-escaped @rawstring extracts nothing when the escaping is wrong
body:
_troubleshooting_

Inspect the stored @rawstring text and match the escaping required by its quoting context. Keep missing captures distinct from null values and verify required capture fields before grouping. A successful extraction stage alone does not establish complete grouped results.

- Caveat: Quoting context decides the escaping: inside a double-quoted regex() string a literal backslash is written with four backslashes and a quote as backslash-quote; inside a /.../ literal the backslash is escaped once. The regex() docs also allow the ASCII code x5c for a backslash.
- Caveat: regex() defaults to strict=true, which drops every non-matching event, so a wrong pattern empties the result. strict=false keeps events and leaves the capture unset; check the extracted field is populated (see cql:pattern:field-presence-vs-total) before grouping.
- Caveat: An unset capture is a silent failure, not an error: do not report 'no matches' until the pattern has been shown to extract on a known-good sample event.
- Caveat: Do not guess the stored form: the raw text may or may not be escaped, and over- or under-escaping both fail. Read one event first.

Example (valid):

```
#repo=example_repo | regex("user\\\\\":\\\\\"(?<user>[^\\\\]+)", field=@rawstring, strict=false) | groupBy([user])
```

Example (ANTI-PATTERN — do not use):

```
#repo=example_repo | regex("user\":\"(?<user>[^\\\\]+)", field=@rawstring, strict=false) | groupBy([user])
```

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:regex`, `cql:syntax:regex-literals`, `cql:troubleshooting:regex-strict-drops-events`, `cql:pattern:field-presence-vs-total`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-regex.html; https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-groupby.html

title: regex() removed events I expected to keep
body:
_troubleshooting_

regex() with the default strict=true filters out every event that does not match the pattern, in addition to extracting capture groups. If you only wanted to extract fields (and keep non-matching events), set strict=false or verify the pattern actually matches.

Example (valid):

```
... | regex("user=(?<user>\\w+)", field=@rawstring, strict=false)
```
Extract without discarding non-matching events.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:regex`, `cql:troubleshooting:strict-false-is-not-a-filter`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-regex.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: timeChart() shows fewer series than expected
body:
_troubleshooting_

timeChart() defaults to limit=10 series when split by a field, silently dropping the rest. If a split has more distinct values than expected but the chart shows only ten lines, raise limit= deliberately.

Example (valid):

```
... | timeChart(span=1h, series=ComputerName, limit=100)
```
Show up to 100 series instead of the default 10.

Applicability: CrowdStrike Query Language

See also: `cql:function:timeChart`, `cql:function:groupBy`

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-timechart.html (reviewed 2026-09-15)

title: drop()
body: Removes the selected field names from each input event. Pass the fields as an array.

title: test()
body: Keeps events whose boolean expression succeeds. Unquoted names inside expressions refer to fields.

title: upper()
body: Computes an uppercase value from a field, with an optional output alias and locale.

title: split()
body: Expands an array into separate events. Optional field selects the array; strip controls prefix removal. This is not string splitting.

title: round()
body: Rounds a numeric value. The how argument chooses round, floor or ceil; as names the output field.

title: array:contains()
body: Filters events using membership of a supplied value in a named array.

title: array:length()
body: Counts flat array elements and optionally names the output field with as.

title: selfJoinFilter()
body: Filters related events using shared fields and where conditions. Prefilter restricts output to events matching the conditions; execution limits still apply.

title: getField() reads a field named by an expression
body:
_function_

Reads the field whose name is the result of source. A literal string names a concrete field; an unquoted identifier reads the field name from that identifier's value. The default output is _getField. It can be embedded in an expression. Computed names require runtime grounding.

Syntax:

```
getField(source, as="_getField")
```

Example (valid):

```
label := coalesce([getField("host-name"), "example.com"])
```

title: Scalar expressions and parameter contexts
body:
The profile provides typed scalar computation, field matching, ordered branches and native assignment/field accessor forms through the existing AST and renderer. Supported filter calls can be expression operands without changing argument types. Literal/glob/regex distinctions and source constraints remain explicit.

Contracts include optional replace.with, required format.field, Boolean kvParse.excludeEmpty, scalar or pairwise rename, literal defaults and expression-valued getField.source. Regex syntax includes shorthand classes and bounded inline i/m/s modifiers. Nullable writes retain incoming-target uncertainty; syntactic capture participation does not establish field presence.

Bare * is the catch-all; quoted "*" remains a value pattern and is not converted to that catch-all. Each source-tag arm applies its own source constraint before grounding. The profile's output and presence rules are conservative implementation choices, not a guarantee of every backend's behavior.

title: Projection and missing-field interpretation
body:
Keep filtering and output projection separate. Inspect projected columns and completeness before interpreting an empty result. Do not equate an absent field with null or infer that an earlier predicate removed an event solely from the shape of projected output.

The profile tracks explicit projected fields and retains uncertainty for unknown output shapes. Static acceptance does not establish a deployment's event-retention behavior.

Sources: https://library.humio.com/crowdstrike-query-language/functions-select.html

title: Aggregate outputs and limits
body:
The profile shares aggregate output metadata between validation and grounding. Collection, selector, stats and top outputs have explicit field contracts. Caps, ordering, ties, approximate precision and grouping ceilings remain diagnostics rather than inferred guarantees.

formatTime requires as in a standalone stage; assignment supplies scalar-output context. Explicit seconds/milliseconds units require signed-long literals, with warnings for dynamic expressions. Distinct requirements and accuracy warnings apply in nested aggregate contexts. Fresh aggregates expire earlier ordering facts.

The profile accepts numeric top.error values and warns on fractional forms. Target support and precision semantics remain deployment dependent; simultaneous sum and max ranking is unsupported.

title: Array bindings, projections and output reuse
body:
The profile represents flat/object array operations through typed calls and inline plans. Element bindings retain their enclosing source; independent query arguments reset scope. Temporary writes remain local. Stream replacement, aggregation, definitions and correlation are excluded from element pipelines, and flat evaluators require an explicit output write on every surviving branch.

Logical arrays and literal scalar fields are tracked separately. A name ending with [] does not establish indexed members. Projection tracks physical fields, while wildcards and dynamic access retain unresolved dependencies. Nullable outputs and reused namespaces do not establish cleanup of other indices.

Use explicit bindings, physical projections and deliberate output names. Unknown structured shapes, gaps and member ownership remain uncertain; the profile does not promise every deployment's runtime array behavior.

title: Joins, tables and enrichment
body:
The profile supports corresponding multikey joins, repo/view and file/table aliases, and bounded table declarations. Declarations use a top-level preamble, explicit includes and at most ten tables; they cannot combine with join/selfJoinFilter. Scalar * selects all table columns, while wildcard list entries remain outside the profile. Match and join have distinct import defaults. Key arity, caps and alias collisions are checked.

Independent searches retain separate target origins from source tags. Unknown imported columns invalidate affected derived facts. Explicit projections can close outgoing uncertainty while earlier dependencies remain recorded. External resources and enrichment availability require deployment context.

Explicit imports preserve owned values, immutable tags and read-only destinations. Unenumerated indexed exports remain unknown; logical containers do not establish ownership of individual or nested members. These are bounded static contracts, not a statement of complete backend behavior.

title: Time functions and correlation
body:
The profile models nullable timestamp/timezone outputs, implicit reads, fixed buckets, series/session outputs and named correlation queries with typed attributes and equality links. Missing dates/years, actual source timestamps, sequence dimensions, target capabilities and temporal ordering remain deployment dependent.

Neighbor placement and order are distinct: an aggregate may provide context without establishing a meaningful order. Correlation aggregation pipelines must be bounded to at most one row. Named queries inherit their continuing source context, while independent searches reset it. Unknown exports cannot establish member presence or absence.

Correlation checks use the same-anchor window policy. Cross-anchor rejection requires explicit event-time sequencing without positive jitter; omitted/custom/ingest dimensions retain uncertainty. Numeric minSpan and other unsupported relative-time forms remain explicit coverage limits.
